title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
section: 3.6 The Main Influences on the Shape of the Yield Curve
text:
3.6 The Main Influences on the Shape of the Yield Curve
In practice, the yield curve shape is driven by three broad forces: expected future rate changes, bond risk premiums, and convexity bias. The observed curve combines all three, so the shape of the curve should not be interpreted as a pure forecast of future short-term rates.

1. The Market’s Expectations of Future Rate Changes
Expected future short-term rates are a major driver of the yield curve. If investors expect central banks to raise policy rates, short- and intermediate-maturity yields usually rise. If investors expect future rate cuts, those maturities usually fall.
The intuition is that a longer-term yield reflects the return from holding a longer bond versus rolling over a sequence of shorter bonds. If the market expects future short rates to be higher, longer yields need to compensate investors for locking in today’s rate.
Examples:

Expected monetary tightening can raise 1-year to 5-year yields and flatten or invert the curve.
Expected monetary easing can pull down 2-year to 5-year yields and steepen the curve.
A recession expectation can lower intermediate and long yields if investors expect future rate cuts.



2. Bond Risk Premiums
Bond risk premiums are the extra compensation investors require for bearing risks that are not captured by expected future short rates. Longer-maturity bonds have more price sensitivity to yield changes, so investors often require a term premium to hold them.
The intuition is that a 30-year bond can lose much more value than a 2-year bond when yields rise. Even if expected future short rates are unchanged, investors may demand a higher long-term yield as compensation for duration risk, inflation uncertainty, liquidity risk, or supply pressure.
Examples:

Higher inflation uncertainty can increase the long-term term premium and steepen the curve.
Heavy long-term Treasury issuance can cheapen long maturities and push long yields higher.
Strong pension or insurance demand for long-duration bonds can lower long-term risk premiums and flatten the long end.
Safe-haven demand can lower Treasury yields, especially in highly liquid benchmark maturities.



3. Convexity Bias
Convexity bias arises because bond prices do not move linearly with yields. Long-duration bonds usually have more convexity, meaning their prices rise more when yields fall than they fall when yields rise by the same amount. This convexity has value.
The intuition is that investors may accept a lower yield on bonds with more desirable convexity, especially when rates are volatile. However, securities with negative convexity, such as callable bonds or mortgage-backed securities, usually require extra yield because their price upside is limited when rates fall.
Examples:

A long Treasury bond may trade at a slightly lower yield than otherwise expected because investors value its positive convexity.
A callable bond may trade at a higher yield because the issuer can call the bond when rates fall.
Mortgage-backed securities can cheapen when rates fall because prepayment risk increases and investors lose some upside.









Category
Main intuition
Example effect




Expectations of future rate changes
The curve embeds expected future short rates
Expected rate cuts can lower intermediate yields


Bond risk premiums
Investors require compensation for duration, inflation, liquidity, and supply risk
Higher inflation uncertainty can raise long yields


Convexity bias
Investors value or penalize nonlinear price behavior
Callable bonds require extra yield for negative convexity











Figure 6: Illustrative effects of rate expectations on the yield curve.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
5.1 Bull Steepener
A bull steepener is a strategy that benefits when yields fall and short-term yields fall more than long-term yields. This often occurs when the market expects central bank easing.
Example position:

long 2-year Treasury notes,
short 10-year Treasury notes in a duration-adjusted amount.







NoteBull Steepener Example



Suppose the 2-year yield is 4.80% and the 10-year yield is 4.20%. The 2s10s slope is:
\[
4.20\% - 4.80\% = -0.60\%.
\]
The curve is inverted by 60 bps. A trader expects recession risk to rise and the central bank to cut rates. One month later:

2-year yield falls to 4.10%,
10-year yield falls to 3.95%.

The new 2s10s slope is:
\[
3.95\% - 4.10\% = -0.15\%.
\]
The curve steepened by 45 bps. A long 2-year / short 10-year duration-neutral trade profits because the long 2-year position gains more from the larger yield decline than the short 10-year position loses.










Figure 8: Bull steepener: yields fall, with the short end falling more than the long end.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
5.2 Bear Steepener
A bear steepener benefits when yields rise and long-term yields rise more than short-term yields. This can occur when inflation risk rises or investors demand a larger term premium.
Example position:

short 30-year Treasury bonds,
long 5-year Treasury notes in a duration-adjusted amount.







NoteBear Steepener Example



The 5-year yield is 4.00% and the 30-year yield is 4.40%, so the 5s30s slope is 40 bps. A trader believes long-term inflation risk is underpriced. Two weeks later:

5-year yield rises to 4.10%,
30-year yield rises to 4.80%.

The 5s30s slope becomes 70 bps. The curve steepened by 30 bps. A short long-bond position gains from the larger yield increase at the long end, while the long 5-year hedge loses less.










Figure 9: Bear steepener: yields rise, with the long end rising more than the short or intermediate sector.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
5.3 Bull Flattener
A bull flattener benefits when yields fall and long-term yields fall more than short-term yields. This often occurs when inflation expectations decline or investors seek duration.
Example position:

long 10-year Treasury notes,
short 2-year Treasury notes in a duration-adjusted amount.

If the 10-year yield falls by 50 bps while the 2-year yield falls by only 15 bps, the long 10-year position gains more than the short 2-year position loses.








Figure 10: Bull flattener: yields fall, with the long end falling more than the short end.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
5.4 Bear Flattener
A bear flattener benefits when yields rise and short-term yields rise more than long-term yields. This often occurs when the central bank is expected to tighten policy.
Example position:

short 2-year Treasury notes,
long 10-year Treasury notes in a duration-adjusted amount.

If the 2-year yield rises by 75 bps and the 10-year yield rises by 25 bps, the curve flattens. The short 2-year position gains more than the long 10-year position loses.








Figure 11: Bear flattener: yields rise, with the short end rising more than the long end.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
5.5 Butterfly Strategy
A butterfly strategy expresses a view on curvature. It compares an intermediate maturity with a weighted average of shorter and longer maturities.
A common 2s5s10s butterfly is:
\[
\text{Butterfly} = 2y_5 - y_2 - y_{10}.
\]
If the 5-year yield is high relative to the 2-year and 10-year yields, the 5-year sector is cheap on the curve. A trader may buy 5-year notes and short 2-year and 10-year notes in duration-adjusted amounts.






NoteButterfly Example



Suppose:



Maturity
Yield




2-year
4.00%


5-year
4.50%


10-year
4.30%



The butterfly is:
\[
2(4.50\%) - 4.00\% - 4.30\% = 0.70\%.
\]
The 5-year point is high relative to the wings. A trader who expects the curve to become smoother may buy the 5-year note and short the 2-year and 10-year notes. If the 5-year yield later falls relative to the wings, the trade profits.










Figure 12: Butterfly trade: the intermediate maturity richens relative to the wings.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
5.6 Carry and Roll-Down
Curve strategies are not driven only by future yield changes. They also earn or lose carry and roll-down.
Carry is the return from holding a position if the yield curve does not change. For a bond, carry includes coupon income minus financing cost.
Roll-down is the price effect from a bond moving to a shorter maturity on an unchanged yield curve. On an upward-sloping curve, a bond may roll down to a lower yield and gain price.






NoteCarry and Roll-Down Example



A 5-year Treasury yields 4.30%. The 4-year point on the curve yields 4.00%. If the curve is unchanged after one year, the bond is now a 4-year bond and its required yield falls by 30 bps. The investor earns coupon income and may also gain from roll-down.
However, if market yields rise enough, the mark-to-market loss can offset the carry and roll-down benefit.

title: Lecture 4: Benchmark Spreads and the Term Structure of Interest Rates
text:
5.7 Risk Controls in Curve Strategies
Curve strategies should be evaluated with explicit risk controls:

duration exposure,
key rate duration exposure,
convexity exposure,
financing cost,
liquidity risk,
stop-loss levels,
scenario analysis.

A trade that appears to be a curve trade may still lose money if it has unintended exposure to the overall level of rates.






WarningImplementation Risk



A duration-neutral steepener is only neutral for small parallel shifts. It can still lose money if volatility rises, financing conditions change, the curve moves in an unexpected maturity sector, or the hedge instrument does not track the cash bond being hedged.

title: Assignment 1 - Easy
text:
This assignment is based on Lectures 1-6: bond features and risks, pricing and yield measures, duration and convexity, benchmark spreads and term structure, Treasury and corporate debt markets, and bond portfolio construction.
The questions are original CFA-style practice questions written from the course material. They are not copied from CFA Institute books or exams.
Questions 1-10 are conceptual, Questions 11-20 are calculations, and Questions 21-25 use the generated spreadsheet files in this folder.


Why does a plain vanilla bond have a predictable cash-flow pattern?
Answer. A plain vanilla bond fixes the coupon rate, coupon dates, face value, and maturity date in the indenture. If the issuer does not default and there is no early redemption, the investor knows both the size and timing of all coupon payments and the final principal repayment. That is why fixed income valuation begins by discounting promised cash flows.



Explain the difference between a fixed-rate bond and a floating-rate note.
Answer. A fixed-rate bond pays the same coupon rate through its life, so its price changes when market yields move away from the coupon. A floating-rate note resets its coupon using a reference rate such as SOFR plus a quoted margin, so its income adjusts with short-term rates. Right after reset, a simple floater often trades close to par if credit spreads are unchanged.



Why does a callable bond usually offer a higher yield than a similar noncallable bond?
Answer. The call option belongs to the issuer and is valuable when rates fall. The issuer can redeem the old high-coupon bond and refinance at lower rates, which limits the investor’s upside and creates reinvestment risk. Investors therefore require extra yield as compensation for giving the issuer that option.



What is credit spread risk?
Answer. Credit spread risk is the risk that the yield spread over a benchmark Treasury or spot curve widens. Even if Treasury rates do not move, a wider spread increases the required yield on the corporate bond and lowers its price. This risk is separate from actual default; a bond can lose value simply because the market demands more compensation for credit or liquidity.



Why should duration not be interpreted as only a measure of time?
Answer. Macaulay duration has time units, but in risk management duration is mainly a measure of price sensitivity to yield changes. Modified duration translates duration into an approximate percentage price change for a small yield change. Two bonds with similar maturities can have very different durations because coupons, yields, and embedded options change the timing and sensitivity of cash flows.



What does positive convexity mean for an option-free bond?
Answer. Positive convexity means the price-yield curve bows outward. For equal-sized yield changes, the price gain when yields fall is larger than the price loss when yields rise. Duration gives the linear first-order effect, while convexity captures the curvature that improves the approximation for larger rate moves.



Why is a spot rate curve better than one yield-to-maturity for valuing a coupon bond?
Answer. A coupon bond has cash flows at many dates. Each cash flow should be discounted at the rate appropriate for its own maturity, so spot rates are conceptually correct. A single yield-to-maturity is a summary discount rate that forces all cash flows to use one rate and can hide errors when the curve is steep or humped.



What is the taxable-equivalent yield of a municipal bond used for?
Answer. It converts a tax-exempt yield into the pretax yield a taxable bond would need to offer to leave the investor equally well off. The formula is tax-exempt yield divided by one minus the marginal tax rate. It matters because investors compare after-tax returns, not only quoted yields.



Why are Treasury bills sold at a discount?
Answer. Treasury bills are zero-coupon securities with maturities of one year or less. They do not pay periodic interest; instead, investors buy them below face value and receive face value at maturity. The difference between purchase price and maturity value is the investor’s interest income.



What is tracking error in bond portfolio construction?
Answer. Tracking error is the standard deviation of active returns, where active return equals portfolio return minus benchmark return. It measures how tightly a portfolio tracks its benchmark. A low tracking error indicates a more passive or benchmark-like portfolio; a high tracking error indicates more active risk.



A 3-year annual-pay bond has face value $1,000, a 5% coupon, and a 6% yield. Compute the price.
Answer. The annual coupon is $50. Price = $50/1.06 + $50/1.06^2 + $1,050/1.06^3 = $973.27. Because the coupon rate is below the yield, the bond sells below par.



Compute the price of a 3-year zero-coupon bond with $1,000 face value and a 4% annual yield.
Answer. The only cash flow is the $1,000 maturity payment. Price = $1,000/(1.04)^3 = $889.00.



A quarterly floater pays SOFR + 150 bps. SOFR at reset is 3.50%. Face value is $1,000. What is the next coupon payment?
Answer. The annual coupon rate is 3.50% + 1.50% = 5.00%. Quarterly payment = 5.00%/4 x $1,000 = $12.50.



A semiannual coupon bond pays $25 every six months. Settlement occurs 30 days after the last coupon in a 180-day coupon period. Compute accrued interest.
Answer. Accrued interest = $25 x 30/180 = $4.17. The buyer pays this amount to compensate the seller for interest earned since the last coupon date.



A 5-year corporate bond yields 5.20% and the 5-year Treasury yields 3.90%. Compute the benchmark spread in basis points.
Answer. Spread = 5.20% - 3.90% = 1.30%, or 130 basis points.



A tax-exempt municipal bond yields 3.20%. The investor’s marginal tax rate is 30%. Compute the taxable-equivalent yield.
Answer. Taxable-equivalent yield = 3.20%/(1 - 0.30) = 4.57%. A taxable bond must yield about 4.57% to match the municipal bond after tax.



A 91-day Treasury bill with $10,000 face value is quoted at a 4.75% bank discount yield. Compute the price.
Answer. Price = $10,000 x [1 - 0.0475 x 91/360] = $9,879.93.



A Treasury note is quoted at 98-24. For $1,000 face value, compute the clean price.
Answer. 98-24 means 98 + 24/32 = 98.75% of par. Clean price = 98.7500% x $1,000 = $987.50.

text:

The questions are original CFA-style practice questions written from the course material. They are not copied from CFA Institute books or exams.
Questions 1-10 are conceptual, Questions 11-20 are calculations, and Questions 21-25 use the generated spreadsheet files in this folder.


Why does a plain vanilla bond have a predictable cash-flow pattern?
Answer. A plain vanilla bond fixes the coupon rate, coupon dates, face value, and maturity date in the indenture. If the issuer does not default and there is no early redemption, the investor knows both the size and timing of all coupon payments and the final principal repayment. That is why fixed income valuation begins by discounting promised cash flows.



Explain the difference between a fixed-rate bond and a floating-rate note.
Answer. A fixed-rate bond pays the same coupon rate through its life, so its price changes when market yields move away from the coupon. A floating-rate note resets its coupon using a reference rate such as SOFR plus a quoted margin, so its income adjusts with short-term rates. Right after reset, a simple floater often trades close to par if credit spreads are unchanged.



Why does a callable bond usually offer a higher yield than a similar noncallable bond?
Answer. The call option belongs to the issuer and is valuable when rates fall. The issuer can redeem the old high-coupon bond and refinance at lower rates, which limits the investor’s upside and creates reinvestment risk. Investors therefore require extra yield as compensation for giving the issuer that option.



What is credit spread risk?
Answer. Credit spread risk is the risk that the yield spread over a benchmark Treasury or spot curve widens. Even if Treasury rates do not move, a wider spread increases the required yield on the corporate bond and lowers its price. This risk is separate from actual default; a bond can lose value simply because the market demands more compensation for credit or liquidity.



Why should duration not be interpreted as only a measure of time?
Answer. Macaulay duration has time units, but in risk management duration is mainly a measure of price sensitivity to yield changes. Modified duration translates duration into an approximate percentage price change for a small yield change. Two bonds with similar maturities can have very different durations because coupons, yields, and embedded options change the timing and sensitivity of cash flows.



What does positive convexity mean for an option-free bond?
Answer. Positive convexity means the price-yield curve bows outward. For equal-sized yield changes, the price gain when yields fall is larger than the price loss when yields rise. Duration gives the linear first-order effect, while convexity captures the curvature that improves the approximation for larger rate moves.



Why is a spot rate curve better than one yield-to-maturity for valuing a coupon bond?
Answer. A coupon bond has cash flows at many dates. Each cash flow should be discounted at the rate appropriate for its own maturity, so spot rates are conceptually correct. A single yield-to-maturity is a summary discount rate that forces all cash flows to use one rate and can hide errors when the curve is steep or humped.



What is the taxable-equivalent yield of a municipal bond used for?
Answer. It converts a tax-exempt yield into the pretax yield a taxable bond would need to offer to leave the investor equally well off. The formula is tax-exempt yield divided by one minus the marginal tax rate. It matters because investors compare after-tax returns, not only quoted yields.



Why are Treasury bills sold at a discount?
Answer. Treasury bills are zero-coupon securities with maturities of one year or less. They do not pay periodic interest; instead, investors buy them below face value and receive face value at maturity. The difference between purchase price and maturity value is the investor’s interest income.



What is tracking error in bond portfolio construction?
Answer. Tracking error is the standard deviation of active returns, where active return equals portfolio return minus benchmark return. It measures how tightly a portfolio tracks its benchmark. A low tracking error indicates a more passive or benchmark-like portfolio; a high tracking error indicates more active risk.



A 3-year annual-pay bond has face value $1,000, a 5% coupon, and a 6% yield. Compute the price.
Answer. The annual coupon is $50. Price = $50/1.06 + $50/1.06^2 + $1,050/1.06^3 = $973.27. Because the coupon rate is below the yield, the bond sells below par.

Answer. The only cash flow is the $1,000 maturity payment. Price = $1,000/(1.04)^3 = $889.00.

Answer. The annual coupon rate is 3.50% + 1.50% = 5.00%. Quarterly payment = 5.00%/4 x $1,000 = $12.50.

Answer. Spread = 5.20% - 3.90% = 1.30%, or 130 basis points.

Answer. Taxable-equivalent yield = 3.20%/(1 - 0.30) = 4.57%. A taxable bond must yield about 4.57% to match the municipal bond after tax.

Answer. Price = $10,000 x [1 - 0.0475 x 91/360] = $9,879.93.

title: Assignment 1 - Medium
text:
This assignment is based on Lectures 1-6: bond features and risks, pricing and yield measures, duration and convexity, benchmark spreads and term structure, Treasury and corporate debt markets, and residential mortgages/MBS.
The questions are original CFA-style practice questions written from the course material. They are not copied from CFA Institute books or exams.
Questions 1-10 are conceptual, Questions 11-20 are calculations, and Questions 21-25 use the generated spreadsheet files in this folder.


A bank portfolio manager says, ‘I prefer floaters because they have no interest-rate risk.’ Evaluate the statement.
Answer. The statement is too strong. Floaters have lower price sensitivity to small parallel shifts shortly after reset because coupons adjust to current short rates, but they still carry spread risk, liquidity risk, cap/floor risk, reset-lag risk, and credit risk. A floater can lose value if the issuer’s required margin widens even when SOFR is unchanged.



Why can a lower-coupon bond have higher duration than a higher-coupon bond with the same maturity?
Answer. Lower coupons push more of the bond’s value into the final principal payment. Because more present value is received later, the weighted average timing of cash flows is later and the price is more sensitive to discount-rate changes. Higher-coupon bonds return more value earlier, which shortens duration.



Explain why pull to par happens when yields are unchanged.
Answer. As maturity approaches, fewer cash flows remain and the principal repayment is less heavily discounted. A discount bond rises toward par because the below-market coupon matters for fewer periods. A premium bond falls toward par because the above-market coupon advantage is being used up.



Why does a callable bond tend to have lower positive convexity than an otherwise identical option-free bond?
Answer. When rates fall, the option-free bond’s price can rise substantially. The callable bond’s price is capped by the increasing probability of being called, so the upside is limited. The issuer’s embedded option therefore subtracts value from the investor and can create negative convexity in the rate region where the call becomes likely.



Distinguish default risk, downgrade risk, and credit spread risk.
Answer. Default risk is failure to make promised payments. Downgrade risk is the risk that a rating agency lowers the issuer’s rating, possibly causing forced selling and higher funding costs. Credit spread risk is the broader market repricing of compensation for credit and liquidity risk; it can occur without default or an actual downgrade.



Why does the on-the-run Treasury curve not always equal the theoretical risk-free discount curve?
Answer. On-the-run Treasuries are the newest and most liquid benchmark issues, so they often trade rich and yield slightly less than comparable seasoned securities. That liquidity premium can contaminate the curve if the goal is pure discounting. A theoretical spot curve tries to infer zero-coupon discount rates across maturities from many prices while controlling for such distortions.



Explain the economic meaning of a forward rate derived from spot rates.
Answer. A forward rate is the break-even reinvestment rate implied by today’s spot rates. If the forward rate from year 1 to year 2 is 5.6%, an investor is indifferent, before risk premiums, between investing for two years directly and investing for one year then reinvesting for the second year at that forward rate. It is not automatically a forecast; it can include term and liquidity premiums.



Why do market-cap-weighted bond indexes have a structural weakness?
Answer. They give the largest weights to the largest borrowers, not necessarily to the safest or most attractive issuers. A heavily indebted issuer can become a larger benchmark constituent precisely because it has issued more debt. This creates an incentive for benchmark-aware managers to hold more exposure to large debtors unless they actively deviate.



Why is average life important for a mortgage pool but insufficient by itself?
Answer. Average life summarizes the weighted timing of principal repayments, which is useful for comparing mortgage pools with prepayments. But two pools can share the same average life while having different month-by-month cash-flow distributions, prepayment convexity, and extension risk. Investors need the full cash-flow path, not only one summary statistic.



What makes a leveraged loan different from a high-yield bond?
Answer. Leveraged loans usually have floating rates, are often senior secured, and sit higher in the capital structure. High-yield bonds usually have fixed coupons, longer maturities, and may be unsecured. The loan has less rate duration but still has credit, liquidity, covenant, and refinancing risk.



A 6-year bond has $1,000 face value, 6% annual coupon paid semiannually, and a 5.20% yield. Compute the price.
Answer. Semiannual coupon = $30, semiannual yield = 2.60%, and there are 12 periods. Price = sum of discounted coupons plus principal = $1,040.78. The bond trades above par because its coupon rate exceeds its yield.



Compute Macaulay and modified duration for a 4-year annual-pay 5% coupon bond yielding 6%.
Answer. Using present-value weights for the four cash flows, Macaulay duration is 3.718 years. Modified duration = Macaulay duration/(1 + y) = 3.507. A 1 bp rise in yield lowers price by roughly 0.0351%.



For the bond in Question 12, use modified duration and convexity to approximate the percentage price change for a 75 bp yield increase.
Answer. Convexity is approximately 16.133. The approximation is -3.507 x 0.0075 + 0.5 x 16.133 x 0.0075^2 = -2.585%. Dollar change is about -24.96.



A 5-year annual-pay bond has a 4% coupon and 5.50% yield. Compute price and identify discount or premium.
Answer. Price = $935.95. It is a discount bond because the coupon rate is lower than the required yield.



Price a 3-year annual-pay 4% Treasury with $1,000 face value using spot rates of 3.50%, 4.00%, and 4.50%.
Answer. Price = $40/1.035 + $40/1.04^2 + $1,040/1.045^3 = $986.98. Each cash flow is discounted at the spot rate matching its date.



A 1-year zero priced at 96.1538 implies z1 = 4.00%. A 2-year 5% annual coupon Treasury with $100 face value is priced at 99.4380. Bootstrap z2.
Answer. Solve 99.4380 = 5/1.04 + 105/(1 + z2)^2. This gives z2 = 5.34%.



The 1-year spot rate is 4.00% and the 2-year spot rate is 4.80%. Compute the one-year forward rate from year 1 to year 2.
Answer. 1 + f = (1.048)^2/1.04, so f = 5.61%. This is the break-even second-year reinvestment rate.



A 182-day T-bill has $10,000 face value and a 5.20% bank discount yield. Compute price and bond-equivalent yield.
Answer. Price = $10,000 x [1 - 0.052 x 182/360] = $9,737.11. BEY = (Face - Price)/Price x 365/182 = 5.41%.



A corporate bond is quoted clean at 101.25% of par with $1,000 face value. Accrued interest is $17.50. Compute full price.
Answer. Clean dollar price is 101.25% x $1,000 = $1,012.50. Full price = $1,012.50 + $17.50 = $1,030.00.



A mortgage pool has beginning balance $750,000, scheduled principal $1,200, and CPR of 9%. Compute SMM and expected prepayment.
Answer. SMM = 1 - (1 - 0.09)^(1/12) = 0.7828%. Prepayment = SMM x ($750,000 - $1,200) = $5,861.92.



Open medium_portfolio_duration.csv. Compute market-value weights and portfolio duration.
Answer. Weights are market value divided by total market value. Total market value is $4,850,000. Portfolio duration is the weighted average: approximately 4.99 years.



Open medium_bootstrap.csv. Bootstrap the 1-year, 2-year, and 3-year annual spot rates from the Treasury prices.
Answer. The 1-year zero gives 4.00%. Using the 2-year coupon bond gives about 4.72%. Using the 3-year coupon bond after discounting earlier coupons gives about 5.14%.



Open medium_spread_duration.csv. Estimate dollar loss for each corporate bond if spreads widen by 40 bps, using spread duration.
Answer. Approximate loss = -spread duration x market value x spread change. The losses are about $19,200, $30,000, and $14,400; total portfolio loss is about $63,600.



Open medium_tbill_quotes.csv. Compute price and bond-equivalent yield for each bill.
Answer. Using the bank discount formula and then BEY formula, the approximate prices are $9,888.75, $9,793.33, and $9,498.33. The corresponding BEYs are about 4.56%, 4.25%, and 5.16%.



Open medium_mbs_cashflows.csv. Compute SMM, prepayment, total principal, and ending balance for each month.
Answer. Apply SMM = 1 - (1 - CPR)^(1/12), prepayment = SMM x balance after scheduled principal, total principal = scheduled principal + prepayment, and ending balance = beginning balance - total principal. The ending balances are approximately $1,192,330, $1,184,071, and $1,174,985.

title: Assignment 1 - Hard
text:
This assignment is based on Lectures 1-6: bond features and risks, pricing and yield measures, duration and convexity, benchmark spreads and term structure, Treasury and corporate debt markets, and residential mortgages/MBS.
The questions are original CFA-style practice questions written from the course material. They are not copied from CFA Institute books or exams.
Questions 1-10 are conceptual, Questions 11-20 are calculations, and Questions 21-25 use the generated spreadsheet files in this folder.


A CIO argues that the safest way to reduce risk is to buy the highest-yielding bonds with the shortest maturities. Give a deep critique.
Answer. Short maturity reduces exposure to level changes in rates, but high yield is often compensation for credit distress, weak liquidity, poor covenants, or near-term refinancing risk. A very short distressed bond can be more dangerous than a longer high-quality bond because the main risk is not duration; it is whether the issuer survives the maturity wall. The correct risk question is which factor is being paid for and whether the spread is enough after expected default loss, downgrade risk, liquidity cost, and portfolio constraints.



Why can a bond’s yield-to-maturity be a misleading measure of expected return?
Answer. YTM assumes promised cash flows are paid, coupons are reinvested at the same yield, and the bond is held to maturity. Those assumptions fail for callable bonds, mortgage-backed securities, distressed bonds, and investors with shorter horizons. Expected return must incorporate reinvestment rates, future sale yield, default probability, recovery, taxes, and embedded option exercise.



Explain why convexity is economically valuable even if two bonds have the same duration and yield.
Answer. If two option-free bonds have the same duration and yield, the more convex bond has a more favorable response to rate volatility: larger gains when yields fall and smaller losses when yields rise. Convexity is valuable because it improves the distribution of price changes. Investors often accept lower yield for more convexity, while callable mortgages may offer more yield because they sell convexity to borrowers.



A portfolio has the same effective duration as its benchmark. Why can it still lose heavily relative to the benchmark when the curve twists?
Answer. Effective duration summarizes sensitivity to a parallel shift. A curve twist changes short, intermediate, and long rates by different amounts. If the portfolio is overweight long key-rate duration and underweight intermediate key-rate duration relative to the benchmark, the same total duration can hide a major mismatch. Key rate duration is needed to expose that curve-shape risk.



Give an intuition for why a theoretical spot curve is a set of discount rates, not a set of expected future short rates.
Answer. Spot rates are today’s prices for zero-coupon cash flows at each maturity. They embed time value, risk premiums, liquidity, financing specialness, and supply-demand effects. Forward rates extracted from spot rates are break-even rates under no-arbitrage pricing, but they are not pure forecasts unless risk premiums are zero and investors are risk-neutral.



Why can a wider spread be rational for a more liquid corporate bond in stressed markets?
Answer. Normally liquidity lowers required yield. In stress, the most liquid bond may be the one investors sell first because it can actually trade, causing its spread to widen faster than illiquid bonds whose prices are stale. The observed spread can therefore reflect immediacy, balance-sheet pressure, and mark-to-market activity, not only fundamental credit deterioration.



Explain the investor’s hidden short option position in a mortgage pass-through.
Answer. The mortgage borrower owns the right to prepay. The MBS investor has effectively sold that option because principal returns when it is least convenient: faster when rates fall and reinvestment yields are low, slower when rates rise and the investor would prefer principal back. This produces negative convexity and makes duration state-dependent.

Answer. Structured products can transform simple loans into tranches with nonlinear exposure to default timing, prepayments, volatility, liquidity, and correlation. A yield pickup may look attractive if the investor models only average loss or average life, while ignoring tail behavior and option exposure. Risk risk is the danger of owning a payoff the investor cannot actually explain under stress scenarios.

Answer. Shareholders benefit from risk-taking because upside is theirs while part of downside is borne by creditors. Negative covenants restrict actions such as additional debt, asset sales, or dividend leakage that would weaken bondholder claims. Strong covenants reduce agency conflict and can lower required spreads; weak covenants leave bondholders exposed to value transfer.

Answer. Both can increase rate exposure, but leverage also introduces financing risk, margin calls, haircut changes, repo rollover risk, and forced-sale risk. title: Assignment 1 - Multistep Hard Problem Set
text:
1.1 Question 1
A private wealth client is considering three newly issued securities. The client understands stock investing but is new to bonds. You are asked to explain the cash-flow mechanics and risk profile before the client chooses one.











Security
Face value
Coupon structure
Maturity
Embedded feature
Other information




A
USD 1,000
5.20 percent fixed annual coupon
8 years
None
Bullet repayment at maturity


B
USD 1,000
3-month SOFR + 1.40 percent, quarterly reset
5 years
Coupon cap at 7.00 percent
Bullet repayment at maturity


C
USD 1,000
6.00 percent fixed annual coupon
10 years
Callable at 102 after year 4
Issuer is expected to refinance if rates decline



Answer the following:

For each security, describe the promised cash-flow pattern before considering default or option exercise.

Identify which security has the most predictable nominal cash flows and explain why.

Identify which security gives the issuer an economically valuable option and explain when that option is most likely to be used.

Explain why Security B may trade close to par after a reset, but still may not be risk-free.

Rank the securities from lowest to highest cash-flow uncertainty for the investor.

Answer.

Security A is a plain fixed-rate bullet bond. It pays USD 52 each year and repays USD 1,000 at maturity. Security B is a floater. Its quarterly coupon changes at each reset based on 3-month SOFR plus 1.40 percent, subject to the 7.00 percent cap, and it repays USD 1,000 at maturity. Security C pays USD 60 each year until maturity unless the issuer calls it after year 4. If called at 102, the investor receives USD 1,020 instead of continuing to receive coupons through year 10.
Security A has the most predictable nominal cash flows. The coupon amount and maturity value are fixed, and there is no embedded option. Security C has fixed coupons too, but the call provision makes the timing of principal repayment uncertain. Security B has uncertain coupons because SOFR changes through time.
Security C gives the issuer the valuable option. The call provision is valuable when market interest rates fall or the issuer’s credit spread tightens enough that it can refinance at a lower cost. In that case, the issuer can redeem the high-coupon bond and replace it with cheaper debt. The investor loses the opportunity to keep earning the 6.00 percent coupon for the full 10 years.
Security B can trade close to par after a reset because the coupon is updated to current short-term rates. If the reference rate resets to market, the coupon is not stale in the way a fixed coupon can be. However, it is not risk-free. Its price can fall if the issuer’s credit spread widens, if liquidity deteriorates, if the coupon cap becomes binding, or if investors require more compensation for the same floater structure.
Lowest uncertainty is Security A because promised nominal cash flows are fixed and bullet-style. Security B is next because the principal timing is fixed but coupons float. Security C has high cash-flow uncertainty because the issuer can change the maturity profile through the call option. If rates fall substantially, the investor should expect early redemption.

title: Assignment 1 - Multistep Hard Problem Set
text:
1.2 Question 2
A junior analyst summarizes bond risks for an investment committee. The committee asks the analyst to classify each event below using the fixed-income risk categories from Lecture 1.







Event
Description




1
Market Treasury yields rise by 90 bps and the price of a fixed-rate bond falls.


2
A BBB industrial bond’s spread over Treasuries widens from 140 bps to 220 bps even though Treasury rates are unchanged.


3
A callable utility bond is redeemed after interest rates fall. The investor must reinvest at lower yields.


4
A high-coupon bond pays coupons as expected, but the investor reinvests those coupons at only 2 percent instead of the 5 percent assumed at purchase.


5
A Canadian investor owns a USD corporate bond and the USD depreciates against CAD.


6
A mortgage-backed security loses value when expected interest-rate volatility rises.



Answer the following:

Assign the main risk category to each event.

For Events 2 and 3, explain why the bond can lose value even if no contractual default occurs.

Explain which two risks can partly offset each other for a buy-and-hold coupon bond.

Identify one event that illustrates risk from an embedded option.

Explain why understanding the security’s structure is itself a risk-control tool.

Answer.

Event 1 is interest-rate risk. Event 2 is credit spread risk. Event 3 is call risk and reinvestment risk. Event 4 is reinvestment risk. Event 5 is exchange-rate risk. Event 6 is volatility risk for an option-rich security.
In Event 2, the market now requires more compensation for credit or liquidity risk, so the required yield rises even though the issuer has not missed a payment. Price falls because the bond’s promised cash flows are discounted at a higher spread. In Event 3, the investor loses because the issuer exercises a contractual right. The issuer pays the call price, so there is no default, but the investor is forced to give up a high-coupon bond and reinvest at lower rates.
Interest-rate risk and reinvestment risk can partly offset each other. When yields rise, the bond’s market price falls, but future coupons can be reinvested at higher rates. When yields fall, the bond price rises, but coupons are reinvested at lower rates. Immunization strategies are built around balancing these two effects for a target horizon.
Event 3 directly illustrates an embedded call option. Event 6 also involves option exposure because prepayment or call behavior becomes more valuable when volatility rises.
Structure matters because cash-flow timing is not always fixed. A bond may be callable, putable, convertible, floating-rate, inverse-floating, amortizing, inflation-linked, or mortgage-backed. If the investor treats all bonds like simple fixed-rate bullets, the investor may misjudge price sensitivity, reinvestment exposure, and downside behavior. This is Fabozzi’s “risk risk”: the risk of not understanding the risks being purchased.

title: Assignment 1 - Multistep Hard Problem Set
text:
1.3 Question 3
An insurance company is comparing a bullet corporate bond with an amortizing asset-backed security. Both securities have final maturities of five years and face values of USD 10,000,000.



Year
Bullet bond principal repayment
ABS principal repayment




1
0
1,200,000


2
0
1,600,000


3
0
2,100,000


4
0
2,500,000


5
10,000,000
2,600,000



Answer the following:

Compute the weighted average life of the bullet bond.

Compute the weighted average life of the ABS.

Explain why the ABS has less principal-timing exposure than the bullet bond even though final maturity is the same.

Explain one risk that could make the realized life of the ABS differ from the scheduled life.

Discuss why a liability-driven investor might prefer the ABS even if its quoted yield is lower.

Answer.

The bullet bond repays all USD 10,000,000 in year 5. Weighted average life equals 5.00 years:

WAL = (10,000,000 x 5) / 10,000,000 = 5.00.

For the ABS:

WAL = (1,200,000 x 1 + 1,600,000 x 2 + 2,100,000 x 3 + 2,500,000 x 4 + 2,600,000 x 5) / 10,000,000.
The numerator is 1,200,000 + 3,200,000 + 6,300,000 + 10,000,000 + 13,000,000 = 33,700,000. WAL = 33,700,000 / 10,000,000 = 3.37 years.

Final maturity only tells us the last date on which principal is repaid. The ABS returns principal throughout the five-year period, so the investor’s capital is recovered earlier on average. Earlier principal recovery reduces exposure to the issuer and to late-period market conditions, but it also creates reinvestment needs.
Prepayments, defaults, recoveries, or collateral performance can change the realized principal schedule. If borrowers prepay faster, WAL shortens. If collateral defaults or extensions delay principal, WAL can lengthen or cash flows can be impaired.
A liability-driven investor may prefer the ABS if its principal payments match expected liability outflows. Matching cash-flow timing can reduce the need to sell assets later. A lower quoted yield may be acceptable if the ABS reduces reinvestment, liquidity, or asset-liability mismatch risk.

Answer the following:

Explain why Treasury yields are often used as benchmark rates.

Explain why the corporate bond should normally trade at a positive spread over Treasuries.

Explain why the municipal bond cannot be compared to a corporate bond only by pretax yield.

Explain why the non-agency RMBS requires analysis beyond a simple issuer rating.

Recommend two due-diligence questions the manager should ask before buying the RMBS.

Answer.

Treasury securities are backed by the sovereign’s taxing authority and are highly liquid. In domestic currency, they are commonly treated as the default-free base rate. Their yields provide a benchmark for the time value of money across maturities.
The corporate bond exposes investors to default risk, downgrade risk, credit spread risk, and lower liquidity than Treasuries. Investors require compensation for those risks, so the corporate yield normally equals the Treasury base rate plus a spread.
Municipal bonds may be tax-exempt. A taxable corporate yield must be converted to an after-tax yield, or the municipal yield must be converted to a taxable-equivalent yield. The investor should compare what is kept after tax, not only the quoted pretax yield.
Non-agency RMBS depends on collateral quality, geographic concentration, loan-to-value ratios, borrower credit quality, prepayment behavior, tranche priority, credit enhancement, and legal structure. A simple rating may not capture the timing and path dependence of losses or prepayments.
First, ask what collateral supports the pool: credit scores, LTV ratios, documentation quality, geography, loan age, and delinquency history. Second, ask how cash flows are allocated across tranches and what stress scenarios have been tested for default, recovery, prepayment, and extension. These questions target both credit risk and structural risk.

title: Assignment 1 - Multistep Hard Problem Set
text:
1.5 Question 5
A high-net-worth investor wants to buy a convertible bond issued by a technology company. The bond has a 2.25 percent coupon, 7-year maturity, and can be converted into 18 shares of the issuer’s common stock. A straight 7-year bond from the same issuer would require a 6.00 percent coupon.
Answer the following:

Explain why the convertible can be issued with a lower coupon than straight debt.

Identify the embedded option and who owns it.

Explain how the bond behaves if the issuer’s stock price rises sharply.

Explain how it behaves if the stock price falls and credit quality weakens.

Compare this convertible bond with an exchangeable bond.

Answer.

Investors accept a lower coupon because they receive potential equity upside through the conversion feature. Part of the investor’s required return is paid in the form of an embedded option rather than current cash interest.
The embedded option is the right to convert the bond into common shares. The bondholder owns this option. It is valuable when the stock price rises enough that the conversion value exceeds the value of remaining bond cash flows.
If the stock price rises sharply, the convertible begins to behave more like equity. Its price becomes increasingly tied to conversion value, calculated as conversion ratio times stock price. The investor benefits from upside that a straight bondholder would not receive.
If the stock price falls and credit quality weakens, the convertible can lose value from both sides. The equity option becomes less valuable, and the bond floor declines as the issuer’s credit spread widens. The investor still has a debt claim, but that claim is only as strong as the issuer’s ability to pay and the bond’s seniority.
A convertible bond converts into shares of the issuer. An exchangeable bond converts into shares of a company other than the issuer. Exchangeable bonds therefore separate issuer credit risk from the equity risk of the reference shares.

title: Assignment 1 - Multistep Hard Problem Set
text:
2.1 Question 6
A student analyst prices a 4-year annual-pay bond with face value USD 1,000 and coupon rate 5.50 percent. The market yield is 6.25 percent.
Answer the following:

Write the cash-flow timeline.

Compute the bond price.

State whether the bond trades at a premium, discount, or par.

Explain the economic reason for the result in part c.

If the yield remains at 6.25 percent, explain the expected direction of the bond’s price as maturity approaches.

Answer.

The bond pays coupons of USD 55 in years 1, 2, and 3. In year 4 it pays the final coupon plus principal, or USD 1,055.
Price = 55 / 1.0625 + 55 / 1.0625^2 + 55 / 1.0625^3 + 1,055 / 1.0625^4.

The present values are approximately 51.76, 48.72, 45.85, and 827.76. Total price is approximately USD 974.09.

The bond trades at a discount.
The coupon rate of 5.50 percent is below the market yield of 6.25 percent. Investors require more return than the bond’s coupon provides at par, so the price must fall below par to raise the expected yield to the market-required level.
If the yield remains constant, the price should pull upward toward par as maturity approaches. The discount exists because the coupon is below market, but as fewer below-market coupons remain, the final principal repayment dominates value.

2.2 Question 7
A bond trader is evaluating a semiannual-pay bond with the following terms:

Compute the number of remaining coupon periods.

Compute the bond price.

Explain why semiannual compounding changes the calculation.

Explain whether this bond should trade above or below par before doing the arithmetic.

Answer.

The semiannual coupon is 7.20 percent / 2 x USD 1,000 = USD 36. The semiannual yield is 6.40 percent / 2 = 3.20 percent.
Six years with two coupons per year gives 12 remaining periods.
Price = 36 x [1 - (1.032)^(-12)] / 0.032 + 1,000 / 1.032^12. The coupon annuity value is approximately USD 355.37 and the principal present value is approximately USD 685.28. Total price is approximately USD 1,040.65.
Semiannual compounding matters because cash flows occur every six months, not annually. The discount rate per period must match the timing of cash flows. Using a 6.40 percent annual discount rate for six annual periods would discount the wrong cash-flow pattern.
The bond should trade above par because its coupon rate of 7.20 percent is above the yield of 6.40 percent. It pays more coupon income than newly required by the market, so investors bid the price above face value.

title: Assignment 1 - Multistep Hard Problem Set
text:
2.3 Question 8
A bond is purchased between coupon dates. It has a 5.00 percent annual coupon paid semiannually on USD 1,000 face value. The quoted clean price is 101.40 percent of par. Settlement occurs 72 days after the last coupon, and the coupon period has 180 days.
Answer the following:

Compute the semiannual coupon payment.

Compute accrued interest.

Compute the clean dollar price.

Compute the full or dirty price.

Explain why the buyer pays accrued interest to the seller.

Answer.

The annual coupon is 5.00 percent x USD 1,000 = USD 50. The semiannual coupon is USD 25.
Accrued interest = 25 x 72 / 180 = USD 10.00.
Clean dollar price = 101.40 percent x USD 1,000 = USD 1,014.00.
Full price = clean price + accrued interest = USD 1,014.00 + USD 10.00 = USD 1,024.00.
The seller held the bond for 72 days of the coupon period and economically earned that portion of the next coupon. Because the next coupon will be paid entirely to the buyer, the buyer compensates the seller through accrued interest at settlement.

title: Assignment 1 - Multistep Hard Problem Set
text:
2.4 Question 9
A client buys a 3-year annual-pay bond for USD 980. The bond has face value USD 1,000 and coupon rate 6.00 percent. The client plans to sell after two years, not hold to maturity. The client expects to reinvest the first coupon at 4.00 percent for one year and expects the bond’s yield at sale to be 5.50 percent.
Answer the following:

Compute the coupon cash flows received during the two-year horizon.

Compute the future value at year 2 of the first coupon after reinvestment.

Compute the expected sale price at year 2.

Compute total future dollars at year 2.

Compute the two-year horizon return.

Answer.

The bond pays USD 60 at the end of year 1 and USD 60 at the end of year 2.
The year-1 coupon is reinvested for one year at 4.00 percent, so its year-2 value is 60 x 1.04 = USD 62.40.
At year 2, the bond has one year remaining and will pay USD 1,060 at year 3. If the sale yield is 5.50 percent, sale price = 1,060 / 1.055 = USD 1,004.74.
Total future dollars at year 2 = reinvested first coupon + second coupon + sale price = 62.40 + 60.00 + 1,004.74 = USD 1,127.14.
The two-year horizon return solves 980 x (1 + R)^2 = 1,127.14. Therefore R = (1,127.14 / 980)^(1/2) - 1 = 7.25 percent approximately. This return differs from the original yield because it depends on the reinvestment rate and sale yield.

title: Assignment 1 - Multistep Hard Problem Set
text:
2.5 Question 10
A firm has issued a floating-rate note with quarterly coupons. The coupon rate each quarter is 3-month SOFR plus a quoted margin of 1.25 percent. The note has face value USD 5,000,000. There is a coupon floor of 2.00 percent and a cap of 6.50 percent. The next three SOFR reset rates are assumed to be:



Quarter
SOFR at reset




1
0.50 percent


2
3.80 percent


3
6.10 percent



Answer the following:

Compute the uncapped annual coupon rate for each quarter.

Apply the floor and cap.

Compute each quarterly coupon payment.

Explain how the cap changes investor exposure.

Explain why discount margin is more natural than yield-to-maturity for this security.

Answer.

The uncapped annual coupon rates are SOFR + 1.25 percent. Quarter 1: 1.75 percent. Quarter 2: 5.05 percent. Quarter 3: 7.35 percent.
The floor is 2.00 percent and the cap is 6.50 percent. Quarter 1 is floored at 2.00 percent. Quarter 2 remains 5.05 percent. Quarter 3 is capped at 6.50 percent.
Quarterly coupon = annual coupon rate / 4 x face value. Quarter 1 = 2.00 percent / 4 x 5,000,000 = USD 25,000. Quarter 2 = 5.05 percent / 4 x 5,000,000 = USD 63,125. Quarter 3 = 6.50 percent / 4 x 5,000,000 = USD 81,250.
The cap limits the investor’s benefit when short rates rise sharply. Without the cap, Quarter 3 would pay 7.35 percent annualized. With the cap, the investor receives only 6.50 percent. The issuer has effectively retained protection against very high reference rates.
Yield-to-maturity assumes a fixed set of cash flows. The floater’s future coupons depend on future SOFR resets and cap/floor behavior. Discount margin frames valuation as a spread over expected reference rates, which better matches the instrument’s economics.

3.1 Question 11
A risk manager studies two annual-pay option-free bonds, each with face value USD 1,000 and yield of 5.00 percent.

Answer the following:

Explain the cash-flow timing intuition behind your prediction.

Compute the approximate price of each bond.

Explain why the lower-coupon bond is more volatile.

State one case where this ranking could fail.

Answer.

Bond X should have greater duration.
Bond X pays small coupons, so more of its value comes from the principal payment at year 10. Bond Y pays larger coupons, which return more value earlier. Duration is based on present-value weighted timing, so the bond with later-weighted cash flows has higher duration.
Bond X price = 20 x [1 - 1.05^(-10)] / 0.05 + 1,000 / 1.05^10 = approximately USD 768.35. Bond Y price = 80 x [1 - 1.05^(-10)] / 0.05 + 1,000 / 1.05^10 = approximately USD 1,231.65.
A small change in yield has a larger effect when more value is concentrated in distant cash flows. Distant cash flows are discounted for more periods, so their present values are more sensitive to the discount rate.
The ranking could fail if the bonds have embedded options or materially different credit behavior. For example, a callable high-coupon bond can have state-dependent effective duration, and an inverse floater can have unusually high duration despite a short contractual maturity.

3.2 Question 12
A portfolio contains three bonds. The manager wants to estimate portfolio duration.

Compute each bond’s market-value weight.

Compute portfolio modified duration.

Estimate the portfolio dollar price change for a 35 bp parallel increase in yields.

Explain one limitation of this estimate for the mortgage pass-through.

Explain how key rate duration could improve the analysis.

Answer.

Total market value is USD 10,000,000. The weights are 40.0 percent Treasury, 35.0 percent corporate, and 25.0 percent mortgage pass-through.
Portfolio duration = 0.40 x 3.8 + 0.35 x 6.2 + 0.25 x 4.4 = 1.52 + 2.17 + 1.10 = 4.79.
Approximate percentage change = -4.79 x 0.0035 = -1.6765 percent. Dollar change = -1.6765 percent x 10,000,000 = approximately -USD 167,650.
The mortgage pass-through has uncertain prepayments. Its duration is not stable because borrower behavior changes when rates move. A static duration estimate can understate extension risk when yields rise or contraction risk when yields fall.
Key rate duration separates exposure by maturity point on the curve. If the portfolio is most sensitive to the 5-year point and the curve twist occurs there, total duration may miss the risk. Key rate duration helps reveal exposure to nonparallel yield-curve changes.

title: Assignment 1 - Multistep Hard Problem Set
text:
3.3 Question 13
A bond’s current price is 104.60. If yield decreases by 50 bps, the model price is 108.90. If yield increases by 50 bps, the model price is 100.55.
Answer the following:

Estimate empirical modified duration.

Estimate empirical convexity.

Use duration alone to approximate the price change for a 75 bp yield increase.

Use duration plus convexity for the same 75 bp increase.

Explain why the two approximations differ.

Answer.

Empirical modified duration = (P_minus - P_plus) / (2 x P0 x shock). The shock is 0.005. Duration = (108.90 - 100.55) / (2 x 104.60 x 0.005) = 8.35 / 1.046 = 7.98.
Empirical convexity = (P_minus + P_plus - 2P0) / (P0 x shock^2). Convexity = (108.90 + 100.55 - 2 x 104.60) / (104.60 x 0.005^2) = 0.25 / 0.002615 = 95.60.
Duration-only percentage change = -7.98 x 0.0075 = -5.99 percent. Dollar price change = -5.99 percent x 104.60 = about -6.26 price points.
Duration-plus-convexity percentage change = -7.98 x 0.0075 + 0.5 x 95.60 x 0.0075^2. The convexity term is about 0.269 percent, so the total is about -5.72 percent. Dollar change = -5.72 percent x 104.60 = about -5.98 price points.
Duration is a linear tangent approximation. Convexity recognizes curvature. For an option-free bond with positive convexity, the convexity term reduces the estimated loss when yields rise and increases the estimated gain when yields fall.

title: Assignment 1 - Multistep Hard Problem Set
text:
3.5 Question 15
A pension plan has liabilities with present value USD 100 million and modified duration 9.0. The asset portfolio has present value USD 100 million and modified duration 6.5. The CIO considers adding Treasury futures to increase duration.
Answer the following:

Explain the duration gap.

Estimate asset value change and liability value change if yields fall by 50 bps.

Explain why the plan’s funded status changes.

Compute the additional dollar duration needed to match liability duration.

Explain why leverage through futures introduces risk beyond duration matching.

Answer.

The assets and liabilities have equal present value, but liabilities are more rate-sensitive. Liability duration is 9.0 while asset duration is 6.5. The plan is under-duration: falling rates increase liabilities more than assets.
Asset percentage change = -6.5 x (-0.0050) = +3.25 percent, or +USD 3.25 million. Liability percentage change = -9.0 x (-0.0050) = +4.50 percent, or +USD 4.50 million.
Funded status worsens because liabilities rise by USD 4.50 million while assets rise by only USD 3.25 million. The plan loses USD 1.25 million of surplus or becomes more underfunded.
Dollar duration needed = (liability duration - asset duration) x asset value = (9.0 - 6.5) x 100,000,000 = USD 250,000,000 duration-dollars per 100 percent yield change. Equivalently, the plan needs USD 25,000 of DV01 because 250,000,000 x 0.0001 = 25,000.
Futures can efficiently add duration, but they introduce margin, basis, roll, liquidity, and operational risks. The futures contract may not perfectly match the liability curve exposure. A hedge can reduce parallel-rate risk while leaving curve, inflation, and collateral risks.

Answer.

Spread = bond yield - Treasury yield. Bond A spread = 0.32 percent = 32 bps. Bond B spread = 0.95 percent = 95 bps. Bond C spread = 3.25 percent = 325 bps.
Different issuers have different default risk, downgrade risk, liquidity, legal protections, and investor bases. Agency debt is close to Treasury quality but less liquid or less explicitly guaranteed depending on issuer. The utility has corporate credit risk. The BB industrial has speculative-grade credit risk and therefore requires much more compensation.
Bond C likely includes the largest credit-risk premium because it is below investment grade and has the widest spread.
Liquidity is a major non-credit reason. A smaller or less frequently traded issue may need a higher yield even if default risk is similar. Tax status, financing eligibility, and embedded options can also affect spreads.
Spread includes expected default loss, risk premium for uncertainty around default, downgrade risk, liquidity premium, tax effects, and sometimes option compensation. Expected default loss is only one component.

Answer.

The 1-year zero price gives z1 = 100 / 96.6184 - 1 = 3.50 percent.
For the 2-year bond: 99.1375 = 4 / 1.035 + 104 / (1 + z2)^2. The first coupon PV is 3.8647. The remaining value assigned to year 2 is 95.2728. Thus (1 + z2)^2 = 104 / 95.2728 = 1.09161, so z2 = 4.48 percent approximately.
For the 3-year bond: 100.1150 = 5 / 1.035 + 5 / (1.0448)^2 + 105 / (1 + z3)^3. The first two coupon present values are about 4.8309 and 4.5804. The remaining value is 90.7037. Thus (1 + z3)^3 = 105 / 90.7037, so z3 = 5.00 percent approximately.
A coupon-bond yield is a single internal rate applied to all cash flows. A spot curve needs a separate discount rate for each maturity cash flow. Coupon yields mix information from multiple cash-flow dates.
Bootstrapping values the earliest cash flows using already solved spot rates. It then solves only for the next unknown spot rate from the remaining price. That prevents the analyst from treating the full coupon bond yield as if it applied directly to every cash-flow date.

Treasury-curve value = 6 / 1.034 + 6 / 1.04^2 + 106 / 1.046^3. This is approximately 5.80 + 5.55 + 92.71 = 104.06.
The corporate bond trades at 101.20, below the Treasury-discounted value of 104.06. That is expected because investors require extra spread for corporate credit and liquidity risk.
With a 60 bp spread, discount rates are 4.00 percent, 4.60 percent, and 5.20 percent. Price is approximately 102.41. With a 90 bp spread, discount rates are 4.30 percent, 4.90 percent, and 5.50 percent. Price is approximately 101.59. A constant spread assumes the same credit spread applies to every cash-flow maturity. Real credit spread curves can slope upward, downward, or change shape across maturities.

4.5 Question 20
A curve strategist observes the following Treasury yields:

The strategist believes the central bank will cut short rates aggressively while long-term inflation uncertainty will keep 30-year yields stable or slightly higher.
Answer the following:

Answer.

The curve is inverted because shorter maturities yield more than longer maturities.
The expected movement is bull steepening: short yields fall substantially while long yields fall less, remain stable, or rise slightly. The curve becomes steeper because the short end declines relative to the long end.
A duration-neutral trade could overweight 2-year Treasuries and underweight 30-year Treasuries, sizing the positions so total dollar duration is approximately neutral. The position profits if 2-year yields fall more than 30-year yields.
The main risk is that the curve does not steepen. If long yields fall more than short yields, the short-2-year/long-30-year relative view loses. If all yields rise, imperfect duration neutrality and convexity differences can also hurt.
Total duration neutrality hedges only a parallel shift. It does not hedge changes in curve shape. A trade can have zero total duration but large positive exposure to the 2-year key rate and large negative exposure to the 30-year key rate.

title: Assignment 1 - Multistep Hard Problem Set
text:
5.1 Question 21
A money-market portfolio buys a 182-day Treasury bill with face value USD 5,000,000 and bank discount yield of 4.80 percent.
Answer the following:

Compute the purchase price using the bank discount formula.

Compute the dollar discount.

Compute the bond-equivalent yield using a 365-day year.

Explain why the bond-equivalent yield is higher than the bank discount yield.

Explain why T-bills are still not riskless for every investor even though they are default-free.

Answer.

Price = Face x [1 - discount yield x days / 360]. Price = 5,000,000 x [1 - 0.048 x 182 / 360] = USD 4,878,666.67.
Dollar discount = 5,000,000 - 4,878,666.67 = USD 121,333.33.
BEY = (Face - Price) / Price x 365 / days. BEY = 121,333.33 / 4,878,666.67 x 365 / 182 = 4.99 percent approximately.
Bank discount yield divides the discount by face value and annualizes on a 360-day basis. BEY divides by the actual investment price and annualizes on a 365-day basis. Because price is below face value, using price as the denominator raises the yield.
T-bills have negligible default risk, but investors can still face reinvestment risk, inflation risk, opportunity cost, and liquidity needs. A foreign investor also faces exchange-rate risk.

Answer.

The USD 1.25 billion enterprise value first pays senior secured claims. The revolver receives USD 200 million and the first-lien term loan receives USD 600 million, leaving USD 450 million. The senior unsecured bonds receive that USD 450 million against USD 700 million of claims. Nothing remains for subordinated notes or preferred equity.
Revolver recovery = 100 percent. First-lien term loan recovery = 100 percent. Senior unsecured bond recovery = 450 / 700 = 64.3 percent. Subordinated notes recovery = 0 percent. Preferred equity recovery = 0 percent.
Actual reorganizations involve negotiation, litigation risk, time value, debtor-in-possession financing, valuation disputes, and the need to gain creditor approval. Some junior claimants may receive value to avoid delay or because valuation is contested.
Secured debt has collateral and senior priority, so expected recovery is usually higher if default occurs. Lower expected loss supports a lower spread. Subordinated debt absorbs losses after senior claims and therefore requires higher compensation.
A limitation on additional secured debt could have protected unsecured bondholders. Without that covenant, the issuer might issue more secured debt ahead of unsecured bonds, reducing their recovery in default.

title: Assignment 1 - Multistep Hard Problem Set
text:
5.4 Question 24
A firm is choosing between commercial paper and a 5-year medium-term note to finance operations.










Instrument

Commercial paper

Medium-term note

Answer the following:

Explain why commercial paper is usually issued at a discount.

Explain why backup bank lines matter for commercial paper issuers.

Explain why an MTN program gives the issuer flexibility.

Explain which instrument creates more refinancing risk.

Explain why the 5-year MTN likely requires a higher yield than 90-day commercial paper for the same issuer.

Answer.

Commercial paper is a short-term zero-coupon or discount instrument. Investors buy it below face value and receive face value at maturity. The discount is the interest earned.
Backup bank lines reassure investors that the issuer can repay maturing paper if the commercial paper market temporarily closes. Without liquidity support, a solvent issuer can still face a rollover crisis.
An MTN program lets the issuer sell notes continuously or episodically with different maturities, coupons, currencies, and structures. The issuer can tailor debt issuance to investor demand and funding needs.
Commercial paper creates more refinancing risk because it matures in 90 days and must be rolled frequently. The MTN locks in funding for five years.
The MTN exposes investors to five years of credit deterioration, interest-rate risk, liquidity risk, and downgrade risk. The 90-day paper has much shorter exposure if it is repaid on time. Investors normally require a higher yield for the longer commitment.

5.5 Question 25
A credit portfolio includes a leveraged loan and a high-yield bond from the same issuer.

Answer the following:

Compare their interest-rate sensitivity.

Compare expected recovery in default.

Explain why the high-yield bond may offer a higher coupon.

Explain one risk in the leveraged loan that is not solved by floating-rate coupons.

Explain how a CLO can transform a pool of leveraged loans into securities with different risks.

Answer.

The leveraged loan has lower interest-rate duration because its coupon resets with SOFR. The high-yield bond has fixed coupons and therefore more price sensitivity to changes in market yields.
The leveraged loan is senior secured, so it usually has higher expected recovery. The high-yield bond is subordinated and unsecured, so it stands behind senior secured claims and likely recovers less in default.
The high-yield bond offers a higher coupon because investors need compensation for fixed-rate duration, lower recovery, subordination, weaker collateral protection, and credit risk.
Floating coupons do not eliminate credit risk. If the issuer’s business weakens, loan price can fall due to wider spreads or higher default probability. The loan can also have liquidity risk, covenant risk, and refinancing risk.
A CLO buys a diversified pool of leveraged loans and issues tranches. Senior tranches have first claim on cash flows and lower risk, while junior and equity tranches absorb losses first and have higher risk. The structure reallocates credit risk rather than eliminating it.

A mortgage underwriter reviews three loan applications.

Answer the following:

Compute each borrower’s PTI ratio.

Compute each borrower’s LTV ratio.

Identify which loan has the strongest basic underwriting profile.

Explain why high LTV increases credit risk.

Explain why credit classification still matters even when LTV is acceptable.

Answer.

PTI = monthly housing payment / monthly income. Borrower A: 2,430 / 9,000 = 27.0 percent. Borrower B: 2,600 / 6,500 = 40.0 percent. Borrower C: 1,850 / 5,000 = 37.0 percent.
LTV = loan amount / appraised value. Borrower A: 480,000 / 600,000 = 80.0 percent. Borrower B: 540,000 / 600,000 = 90.0 percent. Borrower C: 475,000 / 500,000 = 95.0 percent.
Borrower A has the strongest basic profile: prime credit, PTI within common underwriting comfort zones, and LTV of 80 percent. Borrower B has high PTI and high LTV. Borrower C has subprime credit and very high LTV.
High LTV means the borrower has little equity. If home prices fall or foreclosure costs are high, collateral value may not cover the loan. High LTV also weakens the borrower’s incentive to keep paying when financial stress occurs.
Credit classification captures willingness and ability to pay beyond collateral value. Income stability, payment history, documentation, and past delinquencies matter. A borrower with acceptable LTV but weak credit can still default at a high rate.

title: Assignment 1 - Multistep Hard Problem Set
text:
6.2 Question 27
A mortgage pool has beginning balance USD 1,000,000, weighted average mortgage rate 5.40 percent, and scheduled monthly principal of USD 1,800 for the next month. The assumed CPR is 8.00 percent.
Answer the following:

Convert CPR to SMM.

Compute monthly interest.

Compute expected prepayment.

Compute total principal paid.

Compute ending balance.

Answer.

SMM = 1 - (1 - CPR)^(1/12) = 1 - (0.92)^(1/12) = 0.6924 percent approximately.
Monthly interest = beginning balance x mortgage rate / 12 = 1,000,000 x 5.40 percent / 12 = USD 4,500.
Prepayment = SMM x (beginning balance - scheduled principal). Prepayment = 0.006924 x (1,000,000 - 1,800) = approximately USD 6,912.
Total principal paid = scheduled principal + prepayment = 1,800 + 6,912 = USD 8,712.
Ending balance = 1,000,000 - 8,712 = USD 991,288. The investor’s total cash flow for the month before servicing and guarantee fees is interest plus total principal, or about USD 13,212.

title: Assignment 1 - Multistep Hard Problem Set
text:
6.3 Question 28
An agency pass-through investor compares prepayment speeds under 100 percent PSA and 200 percent PSA for a new mortgage pool. Under 100 percent PSA, CPR starts at 0.20 percent in month 1 and rises by 0.20 percent per month until month 30.
Assume beginning balance USD 2,000,000 and scheduled principal USD 2,500 per month for each of the first three months.
Answer the following:

State the CPRs for months 1-3 under 100 percent PSA.

State the CPRs for months 1-3 under 200 percent PSA.

Compute month-1 prepayment under both assumptions.

Explain why 200 percent PSA shortens average life.

Explain why faster prepayments can be bad for an investor holding a premium MBS.

Answer.

Under 100 percent PSA, CPRs are 0.20 percent, 0.40 percent, and 0.60 percent for months 1-3.
Under 200 percent PSA, the CPRs are doubled: 0.40 percent, 0.80 percent, and 1.20 percent.
Month-1 SMM under 100 percent PSA = 1 - (1 - 0.002)^(1/12) = 0.0167 percent approximately. Prepayment = 0.000167 x (2,000,000 - 2,500) = about USD 333. Under 200 percent PSA, SMM = 1 - (1 - 0.004)^(1/12) = 0.0334 percent. Prepayment = 0.000334 x 1,997,500 = about USD 667.
Faster PSA means more principal is returned earlier. Since average life is a principal-weighted timing measure, earlier principal payments reduce average life.
A premium MBS was purchased above par. When borrowers prepay, principal is returned at par, not at the premium price paid. Faster prepayment accelerates premium amortization and forces reinvestment at potentially lower yields.

title: Assignment 1 - Multistep Hard Problem Set
text:
6.4 Question 29
An investor owns two mortgage-backed securities with the same current market value and similar average life, but different coupons.









Pool
Coupon
Current price
Borrower incentive




Low-coupon pool
3.00 percent
91.50
Little refinancing incentive


High-coupon pool
6.50 percent
106.75
Strong refinancing incentive if market rates fall



Answer the following:

Explain which pool is more exposed to contraction risk.

Explain which pool is more exposed to extension risk if rates rise.

Explain why the high-coupon pool may have negative convexity.

Explain why average life alone is insufficient for comparison.

Recommend which pool a bank should prefer if it wants more stable principal cash flows when rates fall.

Answer.

The high-coupon pool is more exposed to contraction risk. If market mortgage rates fall, borrowers with 6.50 percent loans have a strong incentive to refinance, causing principal to return early.
Both pools can extend when rates rise, but the low-coupon pool may be especially extension-prone because borrowers already have below-market mortgage rates and will be reluctant to refinance or move. Principal can remain outstanding longer than expected.
The high-coupon pool has negative convexity because when rates fall, price appreciation is limited by faster prepayments. When rates rise, prepayments slow and duration extends. This is the opposite of the favorable convexity pattern of an option-free bond.
Average life is only a summary. Two pools can have similar average life today but very different sensitivity to future rates, refinancing incentives, burnout, geographic turnover, and borrower behavior.
If the bank wants more stable principal when rates fall, it should prefer the low-coupon pool. Borrowers have little refinancing incentive, so prepayments are less likely to surge in a rally. The bank must still evaluate extension risk under rising-rate scenarios.

title: Assignment 1 - Multistep Hard Problem Set
text:
6.5 Question 30
A mortgage investor evaluates an agency MBS trading at 103.00. The expected cash-flow yield under the base prepayment model is 4.85 percent. Under a faster prepayment model, the yield falls to 4.20 percent. Under a slower prepayment model, the yield rises to 5.05 percent.
Answer the following:

Explain why the same security has different yields under different prepayment assumptions.

Explain why faster prepayments reduce yield for this premium MBS.

Explain why slower prepayments increase yield in this scenario.

Explain why cash-flow yield is limited as a valuation measure.

Explain why option-adjusted spread is often preferred for mortgage-backed securities.

Answer.

A mortgage-backed security’s cash flows depend on borrower prepayment behavior. Cash-flow yield is the discount rate that equates price to one assumed cash-flow path. Change the prepayment path and the timing of principal changes, so the yield changes.
The security trades at 103.00, above par. Faster prepayments return principal at par sooner, forcing the investor to realize the premium faster. The investor also loses higher-coupon cash flows earlier and may reinvest at lower rates. That lowers yield.
Slower prepayments keep the premium security outstanding longer. The investor continues receiving the coupon cash flows for more time, and the premium is amortized more slowly. In this scenario, that raises the modeled yield.
Cash-flow yield assumes the projected prepayment path occurs exactly. It does not fully capture how prepayments change when rates change, nor does it value volatility or the borrower’s prepayment option. It can give false precision.
Option-adjusted spread uses interest-rate scenarios and prepayment behavior linked to those scenarios. It attempts to separate compensation for credit/liquidity spread from the value of the embedded prepayment option. For MBS, that option-aware framework is more informative than a single static cash-flow yield.
